required_edits.relationship: In ‘Disease in History: Frames and Framers’ (1989) Rosenberg calls the social construction of illness ‘in an important sense … no more than a tautology’, avoids the term because it overemphasizes functionalist ends and arbitrariness, and argues that the main trends in the history of disease, social-control readings among them, lose sight of the process of disease definition itself and its consequences.
required_edits.evidence_note: His own text, read in the Milbank Memorial Fund's open archive copy of The Milbank Quarterly 67, Suppl. 1 (1989), pp. 1–15. p. 2: ‘Much has been written during the past two decades about the social construction of illness. But in an important sense this is no more than a tautology’; the position ‘still serves to remind us’ that medical thought is rarely free of social constraint. p. 3: ‘I have, in fact, avoided the term social construction. I felt it has tended to overemphasize functionalist ends and the degree of arbitrariness’ and focused on ‘a handful of socially resonant diagnoses’; he uses ‘the less programmatically charged metaphor “frame”’. pp. 3–4 list five trends in disease history (social history; public health and the demographic transition; an ecological ‘new materialism’; demography; and, ‘perhaps most widely influential’, disease definitions as ‘a tool of social control’, citing Wright and Treacher 1982 and Figlio 1978, in which physicians are construed as agents of ‘a broader hegemonic enterprise’); p. 4: ‘What is often lost sight of in each of these emphases—and in the aggregate in all—is the process of disease definition itself’ and its consequences. The ‘lost sight of’ sentence applies to all five trends, not to social-control readings alone. A critique within a field he also built (his contribution edge edge_2946 remains): it qualifies the constructionist and social-control strands of medical history, it does not reject social history of medicine, which he calls necessarily ‘social’ (p. 3). The essay was reprinted as the introduction to Framing Disease (with Janet Golden, 1992) and in Explaining Epidemics (1992); those reprints were not collated. Named targets (Wright, Treacher, Figlio) are not atlas endpoints.
